b: p
It’s five answers to five questions. Here we go…
h
1. Is my boss telling me to stop doing my coworker’s job?
q

Last year I was assigned to help with a senior engineer’s project because it was too much for one person. He’s technically both the team lead (TL) and owns one of our seven systems, but he’s not always good at distinguishing which hat to wear. I don’t think TL is bad at his job, per se — he’s very good technically with the system, but he doesn’t actively pursue the ‘lead’ side of things.
q

I’ve been taking on some of the lead work he should be doing, like coordinating with our team members to remove obstacles and facilitate work, and performing quality alignments on our combined deliverables. He’s also away from his desk frequently — it’s not unusual for someone to contact me because they have questions and can’t get in touch with him.
q

My manager has noticed the responsibility shift. During our previous one-on-one, she said it seems I’ve been doing a fair bit of the work. I appreciated that she saw it — TL has been out during the review period for the last few assignments, and I put in a lot of solo effort to finalize them before the release. However, she implied that I was more deeply embedded than she wanted me to be. This time, she gently pointed out I seem to have become the point person for the team … but that what I’m doing is something someone else can do, that it isn’t something I need to be doing.
q

I’m confused as to whether this is negative feedback. Is she politely telling me to stay in my lane because I’ve overstepped? Or is she nudging me away from unfair work distribution? I know she has concerns about my workload — on paper, I have more projects than the others, though overall they’re smaller and simpler and I would argue I have the lightest workload. I’ve been consistently meeting my deadlines.
q

My previous attempts to untangle myself from the extra responsibilities (“we agree on XYZ — are you good to take that action or do you need support?”) haven’t gotten me very far. It feels like I end up trying to puppeteer from the sideline, and eventually I get pulled back in.
q

It would be easier to let go if I could be fully uninvolved with this team, but there’s an assignment in the pipeline that would be a great development experience for me. Until then, I’m not sure how to keep the roles from blurring. TL is very passive, and I get frustrated — some the these are things that, if not addressed now, will bite us later. Conceptually, I know, I am the swimmer in the wrong lane. But I don’t know how to course correct without making the team (and the project) flounder.
p

Just based on what’s here, it sounds like your manager is indeed telling you that she wants you to pull back from doing TL’s job. Maybe that’s because by stepping in, you’re preventing her or others from clearly seeing what TL is and isn’t doing (and thus from addressing those issues with him). Maybe it’s because she’s worried about fair division of work. Maybe it’s because it’s just not your job and she doesn’t want you doing it. Regardless of the reason, it does sound like she’s telling you to stop.
p

If you’re not sure that that was the message, you should go back and ask more directly because if she is telling you to stop, you don’t want to just ignore that. You’re asking whether her feedback is negative (“you’ve overstepped” vs. “you’re a huge help but the extra workload is unfair for you to have to take on”) and sure, that’s a useful nuance … but with either one of those, the message would still be to stop, and I think you might be glossing over that.
p

You mentioned you’re unsure of how to pull back without it harming the team, but that’s for her to figure out, not you. However, if you want to have that discussion with her, you definitely can! Frame it as, “I’m concerned that if I hadn’t done X on the Y project, Z would have happened — should I really just let that rope drop in the future?” But if she says yes, then you really do need to do that.
h
2. My coworker and I had a screaming match over the post office schedule
q

I work at a law firm, and the runner we had for a while left to go to college. Since then, the receptionist is to go three days a week to the post office while the other paralegal, Jane, and I are to go one day each. It’s important to note this schedule came from the president of the firm. Jane has decided that the receptionist is to go two days a week, with alternating two days between herself and me. We actually got into a yelling match when I told her she wasn’t my boss nor my manager. I also asked the boss who came up with this plan, and he told both of us his schedule for this.
q

A couple of weeks pass, and Jane corners me in the lobby with the receptionist to tell me I need to go again this week. I, politely, told her that the attorney said otherwise and that, until he tells me otherwise, I’m not doing that. She got mad and stormed off.
q

I honestly have no idea how to handle this. It needs to be shut down but not sure how to go to my boss and let tell him she’s started it all over again. This is absolutely beyond stupid, if you ask me.
p
Yeah, don’t get into a shouting match with a coworker — about anything, but particularly about this.
p

Proactively go and talk to Jane and say this: “I’m sorry our last conversation got heated; that shouldn’t have happened. I’ve been following Rupert’s instructions for our schedule. Have you been given different instructions about how we’re supposed to handle this?” Then, depending on what she says, you could say, “Why don’t we both talk to him together so that we all have the same information on how he wants it done?” If Rupert doesn’t have any authority over Jane or the process itself, then you could say, “Rupert has clearly told me that he only wants me to do it once a week. You can talk to him directly if you want to, but I can’t go against what he’s told me to do.”
p

If there’s a possibility Jane will talk Rupert into doing it her way and you don’t want that, talk to Rupert first and explain why you’re opposed to that, so that he already has that info before she approaches him.
p

You also might ask Jane, if you haven’t already, what’s behind her attempts to change the schedule. It’s possible there’s some piece of info that would shed light on why she keeps pushing this — but even if there’s not, you should make a good-faith attempt to understand where she’s coming from, for the good of your overall reputation in your office if nothing else.
h
3. Did googling weird eggs on my work computer look like something very different?
q

I wanted to ask about something weird that happened on my work computer. My coworker owns chickens and was talking about how one hen was laying weird eggs. He had described them as oddly shaped and textured, but he didn’t give further details. I was helping him troubleshoot by googling what might cause hens to lay weird eggs.
q

I sent him photos through Teams of oblong eggs, eggs with twists and tails, and lash eggs (ugly, wrinkled eggs resulting from an internal infection). Suddenly, my internet was cut off from my work computer for 10 minutes, and nobody else was experiencing the same connection issues as me.
q

I found it to be very odd, until I realized that the eggs in the photos that I sent him were vaguely long and skin-colored. Is it possible that IT has an internal software that flags potentially inappropriate photos shared on the work computer? I never got a message from my manager or IT, but did they shut down my internet remotely to see if I was sharing penis photos to my coworker? Is it possible for them to do that? For the record, I’m a cis woman with no penis to take photos of.
p
It’s possible! And then someone would have reviewed it, seen that it was weird eggs and not penises, and determined all was well.
h
4. What nonprofit jobs exist other than fundraising?
q

I am a teacher seriously thinking about transitioning out of the classroom. Lots of the online guides and articles for transitioning teachers say that other nonprofit work can be a good fit and fulfill the part of you that likes making a difference. However, all of the non profit job boards I’ve looked at seem to only have budgetary and fundraising job opportunities available. I understand that this is a very necessary aspect of nonprofit work; however, fundraising and finances are really not for me. What are other higher level jobs in nonprofits that I could be looking for?
p

Nonprofits hire people to do all the same jobs as for-profit businesses do: web design, accounting, research, management, communications, administrative work, I.T., lobbying, HR, and on and on. But on top of that, they also have additional roles like grant writers, volunteer coordinators, and community organizers.
p

A teaching background could be a good match with a lot of jobs that many nonprofits have: community outreach (designing or doing), training, program development, and possibly even grant-writing (you said you’re not interested in fundraising, but grant-writing is a different type of fundraising than you might be envisioning, and teachers often have experience developing persuasive written materials and clearly communicating goals and outcomes). There are also nonprofit jobs that even more directly intersect with teaching, like working with students outside of a traditional academic setting, curriculum development, education policy, and working for mission-driven organizations within the education space.
p

Also, what were you teaching? The subject matter itself might point you in a direction related to that specific topic. For example, if you taught science, you might look at environmental education or science communication.
h
5. Telling people I’m leaving without drawing all the attention at our annual picnic
q

I am resigning from my role about two months from now, and submitted my resignation to my boss this week. He has been very good to me, I provide an internal service across our group, I am leaving to complete a degree, and I am appreciated in my office; hence the long notice.
q

We have our annual picnic next Thursday, and I would like to not share with my coworkers until after the picnic to avoid the hullaballoo and to keep the focus on our retirees. However, is this odd and am I overthinking it? It also eats up a week of planning, so I could start telling people discreetly now as well.
p

You’re probably overthinking it; there is unlikely to be a hullaballoo at the picnic unless you announce it that same day. Announce it earlier and it’s unlikely to become the focus in a significant way.
